# Chapter 7: Exceptions — 7.1–7.2

Rules that no analyzer enforces (judgment), CONSIDER rules that analyzers only suggest, and rules that analyzers check only in part, marked "(partly checked)". Open the examples file for the explanation and code the book gives with each rule.

## 7.1 Exception Throwing

- **FDG7001** DO NOT return error codes. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7001
- **FDG7002** DO report execution failures by throwing exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7002
- **FDG7003** CONSIDER terminating the process by calling `System.Environment.FailFast` instead of throwing an exception if your code encounters a situation where immediate process termination is necessary. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7003
- **FDG7004** DO NOT use exceptions for the normal flow of control, if possible. Prefer Tester–Doer or the Try pattern to throwing exceptions in common cases. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7004
- **FDG7005** CONSIDER the performance implications of throwing exceptions. Throw rates greater than 100 per second are likely to noticeably impact the performance of most applications. See section 7.5 for details.
- **FDG7006** DO document all exceptions thrown by publicly callable members because of a violation of the member contract (rather than a system failure) and treat them as part of your contract. (library only) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7006
- **FDG7007** DO NOT have public members that can either throw or not throw based on some option. (partly checked) (library only) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7007
- **FDG7008** DO NOT have public members that return exceptions as the return value or an `out` parameter. (partly checked) (library only) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7008
- **FDG7009** CONSIDER using exception builder methods. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7009
- **FDG7010** DO NOT throw exceptions from exception filter blocks. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7010

## 7.2 Choosing the Right Type of Exception to Throw

- **FDG7012** DO NOT create new exception types to communicate usage errors. Throw one of the existing base library exceptions instead. See section 7.3 for detailed usage guidelines for the most common standard exception types. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7012
- **FDG7013** CONSIDER creating and throwing custom exceptions if you have a program error condition that can be programmatically handled in a different way than any other existing exception. Otherwise, throw one of the existing exceptions. See section 7.4 for details on creating custom exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7013
- **FDG7014** DO NOT create a new exception type if the exception would not be handled differently than an existing framework exception. Throw the existing framework exception in such case. See section 7.3 for detailed usage guidelines for the most common standard exception types. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7014
- **FDG7015** DO create a new exception type to communicate a unique program error that cannot be communicated using an existing framework exception. See section 7.4 for details on creating custom exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7015
- **FDG7016** AVOID creating APIs that when called can result in a system failure. If such a failure can occur, call `Environment.FailFast` instead of throwing an exception when the system failure occurs. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7016
- **FDG7017** DO NOT create and throw new exceptions just to have your feature name in the exception type or namespace name.
- **FDG7018** DO throw the most specific (the most derived) exception that makes sense. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7018

## 7.2.1 Error Message Design

- **FDG7019** DO provide a rich and meaningful message text targeted at the developer when throwing an exception. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7019
- **FDG7020** DO ensure that exception messages are grammatically correct. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7020
- **FDG7021** DO ensure that each sentence of the message text ends with a period. (partly checked) (not in test projects) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7021
- **FDG7022** AVOID question marks and exclamation points in exception messages. (partly checked) (not in test projects)
- **FDG7023** DO NOT disclose security-sensitive information in exception messages.
- **FDG7024** CONSIDER localizing the exception messages thrown by your components if you expect your components to be used by developers speaking different languages. (library only) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7024

## 7.2.2 Exception Handling

- **FDG7025** DO NOT swallow errors by catching nonspecific exceptions, such as `System.Exception`, `System.SystemException`, and so on, in framework code. (partly checked) (library only) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7025
- **FDG7026** AVOID swallowing errors by catching nonspecific exceptions, such as `System.Exception`, `System.SystemException`, and so on, in application code. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7026
- **FDG7027** DO NOT exclude any special exceptions when catching for the purpose of transferring exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7027
- **FDG7028** CONSIDER catching a specific exception when you understand why it was thrown in a given context and can respond to the failure programmatically. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7028
- **FDG7029** DO NOT overcatch. Exceptions should often be allowed to propagate up the call stack. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7029
- **FDG7030** DO use try-finally and avoid using try-catch for cleanup code. In well-written exception code, try-finally is far more common than try-catch. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7030
- **FDG7032** DO use `ExceptionDispatchInfo` when rethrowing an exception from a different context. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7032
- **FDG7033** DO NOT handle non-CLS-compliant exceptions (exceptions that don’t derive from `System.Exception`) using a parameterless catch block. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7033

## 7.2.3 Wrapping Exceptions

- **FDG7034** CONSIDER wrapping specific exceptions thrown from a lower layer in a more appropriate exception if the lower layer is just an implementation detail for the operation. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7034
- **FDG7035** AVOID catching and wrapping nonspecific exceptions. — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7035
- **FDG7036** DO specify the inner exception when wrapping exceptions. (partly checked) — examples: examples/ch07-exceptions-7-1-to-7-2.md#fdg7036
